title: Menopause hormone therapy: an individual decision
intro: Menopause hormone therapy can relieve troublesome hot flushes, night sweats and some related symptoms. It is an option, not an obligation. Benefits and risks depend on age, medical history, formulation and route, and deserve individualized discussion.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem
paragraphs: Systemic treatment works throughout the body; low-dose vaginal estrogen mainly treats local dryness and discomfort and has a different risk profile. A person with a uterus usually needs endometrial protection with systemic estrogen.

sections.heading: Assessment and tests
paragraphs: Assessment includes symptoms, unexplained bleeding, breast history, clotting risks, liver health and medicines. Hormone tests are not always necessary for typical menopause. Discuss early menopause separately because treatment goals can differ. Bring your medicine list and previous results; ask which findings would change the plan.

sections.heading: Treatment choices
paragraphs: Options include tablets, patches or gels with appropriate progestogen when needed; nonhormonal approaches are also available. Oral and transdermal estrogen have different clot risks. Do not assume compounded or herbal hormones are automatically safer. Agree how benefit and adverse effects will be checked before changing treatment.

sections.heading: Everyday care
paragraphs: Agree symptom goals and regular review of dose, side effects and continuing benefit. There is no single stopping date suitable for everyone. Hormone therapy is not contraception; discuss pregnancy prevention when still relevant. Choose a routine you can maintain, and discuss barriers such as cost, work or language.

sections.heading: Follow-up and warning signs
paragraphs: Unexplained bleeding needs assessment before treatment, and new or persistent bleeding during therapy should be reported. Chest pain, severe breathlessness, a swollen painful leg or stroke symptoms require urgent help rather than waiting for review.

examples.title: A practical example
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Mira has sleep-disrupting hot flushes and asks about patches, tablets and nonhormonal choices, weighing her own risk rather than a friend’s prescription.

examples.title: Another practical example
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Arben supports a partner in keeping a symptom record. She discusses persistent bleeding with the prescriber instead of assuming every change is normal menopause.
